claim: Across top schools, the dominant 'Why Us' supplement failure mode is the copy-paste/swap-the-name essay: praise for prestige and a list of programs with no demonstrated engagement, sometimes literally naming the wrong school. Practitioners (incl. a former Pomona associate dean of admissions) and University of Michigan's own prompt agree a strong 'Why Us' is bidirectional - specific institutional fit AND what the student will contribute - not flattery.

application.content: The copy-paste test: if a sentence in a 'Why Us' essay would remain TRUE after swapping in a peer school's name, delete or replace it. Every retained claim should be (a) specific to this institution and (b) tied to something real about the student (a goal, a habit, a prior project). Aim for a two-way street - what the student will do WITH the resource and contribute, not just admiration of it. Michigan's prompt makes this explicit: 'How would that curriculum support your interests?'

Before (weak): 'Michigan's world-class faculty and vibrant community will help me achieve my dreams.' (Swap-able; flattery; no contribution.) After (strong): names a specific Michigan program/curriculum feature, states the writer's concrete interest it serves, and what the writer would do or build there - so it answers 'how would that curriculum support your interests' and shows engagement, not prestige-worship.

connections.note: Yale's 'Why Yale' is a concrete instance of this rule.
MIT's field-of-study prompt is a miniature Why-Us subject to the same fit-evidence rule.
Why-Us (institution fit) and Why-Major (intellectual engagement) are paired but distinct failure modes.

provenanceTrail: Craft claim verified at the Tier-2 bar (x2 independent): named former Pomona associate dean (Dr. Tina Brooks via Top Tier Admissions, on-record, dated Aug 2024) on authenticity/fit-evidence/no-resume-recap, plus University of Michigan's official prompt language operationalizing the two-way 'how would that curriculum support your interests' framing (Tier-1 institution, mirrored via CollegeVine for word count). The 'wrong school name' / copy-paste failure mode is widely attested practitioner knowledge; framed here as semi-stable craft, not a volatile single-prompt fact.
